pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify and discuss various strategies of conserving energy.

pages.title: What Does Conserving Energy Mean?
pages.body: Conserving energy means deliberately reducing how much energy is used to carry out a task, without giving up the benefit the task provides, usually by avoiding waste or by choosing more efficient equipment and habits. This is different from generating energy or converting it from one form to another, since conservation is specifically about using less energy overall for the same result.

pages.title: Ironing in Bulk
pages.body: Ironing in bulk means collecting several garments together and ironing them all in one session, rather than heating the iron separately for just one or two items at a time. Since an electric iron uses a significant amount of energy simply to heat up before any ironing can begin, ironing many garments during a single period of heating uses far less total energy than repeatedly heating and cooling the iron for small, separate batches.

pages.title: Using Energy Efficient Appliances
pages.body: Energy efficient appliances are designed to perform the same task, such as lighting a room or cooling food, while consuming less electrical energy than older or less efficient alternatives. Energy saving bulbs, for example, produce the same amount of light as older incandescent bulbs while converting a much smaller proportion of their electrical energy into wasted heat. Choosing appliances labelled as energy efficient, where available, is a simple, ongoing way to reduce a household's overall energy consumption without changing daily habits significantly.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Switching Off Appliances When Not in Use

pages.title: Switching Off Appliances When Not in Use
pages.body:
Switching off lights, fans, televisions and other appliances whenever they are not actually needed prevents energy from being used, and therefore wasted, for no benefit. Some appliances left plugged in, even while switched off at the appliance itself, can still draw a small amount of standby power, so switching off at the wall socket, where practical, can conserve even more energy over time.

[[pic:A simple household scene split into two panels, the left panel labelled Wasteful Habits showing a room with lights on in an empty space, a television left on with no one watching, and several small ironing sessions happening on different days, and the right panel labelled Energy Conserving Habits showing lights switched off in an empty room, an energy efficient bulb, and a single large pile of clothes being ironed together in one session.]]

Notice how the same basic activities, lighting a room, watching television, and ironing clothes, can be carried out in ways that either waste energy or conserve it, without necessarily requiring any new equipment beyond a simple change in habit.

pages.title: Other Everyday Strategies for Conserving Energy
pages.body: Beyond the three strategies specifically named in the curriculum, several other everyday habits also conserve energy effectively. Using natural daylight instead of electric lighting during the day, setting refrigerators and freezers to sensible temperatures rather than colder than necessary, keeping doors and windows closed when air conditioning or fans are running, and maintaining vehicles and appliances properly, since poorly maintained equipment often uses more energy than well maintained equipment doing the same job, are all additional strategies worth discussing alongside the three highlighted in this lesson.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Governments and utility companies in many countries, including Ghana, sometimes run public awareness campaigns encouraging households and businesses to adopt energy conserving habits, particularly during periods of high electricity demand, since conserving energy at a national level can reduce strain on the electricity supply and lower costs for everyone.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Importance of Energy Conservation in Daily Life

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Research information about energy conservation and discuss its importance to life.

pages.title: Economic Importance of Energy Conservation
pages.body: Conserving energy directly reduces the amount households, schools and businesses spend on electricity and fuel, since using less energy for the same task naturally lowers utility bills and running costs over time. For a country as a whole, widespread energy conservation can reduce the total demand placed on the national electricity supply, potentially lowering the need for expensive new power generation and reducing the frequency of power shortages during periods of especially high demand.

pages.title: Environmental Importance of Energy Conservation
pages.body: Since a significant share of the world's energy still comes from burning fossil fuels, conserving energy directly reduces the amount of fuel that needs to be burnt, which in turn reduces the release of greenhouse gases and other pollutants linked to climate change and air pollution, topics studied in an earlier grade. Energy conservation is therefore one of the most immediately available actions individuals and communities can take to reduce their environmental impact, without needing to wait for new technology or infrastructure.

pages.title: Importance for Resource Sustainability
pages.body: Non renewable energy sources, such as coal, crude oil and natural gas, exist in limited supply and cannot be replaced on a human timescale once used up. Conserving energy helps extend how long these limited resources remain available, giving more time for renewable energy technologies to develop and become more widely accessible, and reducing the pressure to rapidly extract remaining non renewable reserves.

pages.title: Social and Community Importance
pages.body:
Communities that conserve energy collectively can help ensure a more reliable, stable electricity supply for everyone, since excessive demand at peak times can strain electricity grids and lead to power outages that affect hospitals, schools, businesses and households alike. Energy conservation habits learnt at home or in school can also spread through a community as people share and model good practices with family, friends and neighbours.

[[pic:A simple infographic style diagram with a central label reading Importance of Energy Conservation, connected by four labelled branches to Lower Costs, Reduced Environmental Harm, Extended Resource Availability, and Reliable Community Supply, each branch illustrated with a small representative icon.]]

Notice how a single, simple action, conserving energy, connects to benefits across four very different areas, economic, environmental, resource related and social, which is why energy conservation is emphasised so strongly across households, schools, businesses and national policy.

pages.title: Researching and Discussing Energy Conservation
pages.body: Reliable information about energy conservation can be found through government energy agency publications, educational websites, and reputable news sources discussing national or global energy policy. When researching this topic, it is useful to look specifically for information connecting energy conservation to cost savings, environmental protection, and resource sustainability, since these three themes, together with social and community benefits, capture most of the reasons energy conservation matters in daily life.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Some countries have introduced financial incentives, such as reduced taxes on energy efficient appliances, or penalties for excessive energy use during peak demand periods, specifically to encourage greater energy conservation among households and businesses. These policies illustrate how the importance of energy conservation extends beyond individual habits into national economic planning.

pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Calculate electrical energy consumed by the use of electrical appliances in kilowatt hour (kWh), using P = IV, where P is power, I is current, and V is voltage.

pages.title: Electrical Power
pages.body: Electrical power is the rate at which an appliance converts electrical energy into another useful form, such as light, heat or motion, and is measured in watts. Electrical power can be calculated using the formula power equals current multiplied by voltage, often written as P equals I multiplied by V, where P is power in watts, I is current in amperes, and V is voltage in volts. Most household appliances have their power rating printed on a label, usually stating how many watts, or kilowatts, the appliance uses when running.

pages.title: Energy Consumed Over Time
pages.body: Electrical energy consumed is the total amount of electrical energy an appliance uses over a period of time, and is calculated by multiplying the appliance's power by the length of time it is used. When power is measured in kilowatts and time in hours, the resulting unit of energy is the kilowatt hour, commonly abbreviated kWh, which is the standard unit used on electricity bills. The general formula is energy consumed equals power multiplied by time, or energy (kWh) equals power (kW) multiplied by time (hours).

pages.title: Worked Example
pages.body:
Consider an electric iron rated at 1000 watts, used for 2 hours. First, convert the power to kilowatts by dividing by 1000, giving 1000 watts divided by 1000 equals 1 kilowatt. Next, multiply the power in kilowatts by the time in hours, giving 1 kilowatt multiplied by 2 hours equals 2 kilowatt hours. This means the iron consumes 2 kWh of electrical energy during that 2 hour period.

Consider a second example, a ceiling fan rated at 75 watts, used for 8 hours. Converting to kilowatts gives 75 watts divided by 1000 equals 0.075 kilowatts. Multiplying by the time gives 0.075 kilowatts multiplied by 8 hours equals 0.6 kilowatt hours, meaning the fan consumes 0.6 kWh of electrical energy over that period.

[[pic:A worked calculation diagram showing an electric iron with a label reading 1000 W, an arrow to a conversion step showing 1000 W divided by 1000 equals 1 kW, then a second arrow showing 1 kW multiplied by 2 hours equals 2 kWh, with each step clearly boxed and labelled.]]

Notice that the calculation always follows the same two steps, converting power to kilowatts if it is given in watts, then multiplying by the number of hours the appliance is used, to arrive at the total energy consumed in kilowatt hours.

pages.title: Energy Consumption of Several Appliances
pages.body:
Comparing the energy consumption of different household appliances over a typical period of use shows clearly why some appliances contribute far more to an electricity bill than others, even if they seem similar in size, as shown in the table below.

| **APPLIANCE** | **POWER (WATTS)** | **TIME USED (HOURS)** | **ENERGY USED (kWh)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Electric iron** | 1000 W (1 kW) | 2 hours | 2 kWh |
| **Ceiling fan** | 75 W (0.075 kW) | 8 hours | 0.6 kWh |
| **Television** | 150 W (0.15 kW) | 4 hours | 0.6 kWh |
| **Refrigerator** | 200 W (0.2 kW) | 24 hours | 4.8 kWh |

Notice that the refrigerator, despite having a relatively low power rating compared with the iron, consumes the most total energy in this comparison, since it typically runs for a full 24 hours every day, illustrating that both power rating and total time of use matter when estimating energy consumption.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Electricity companies use the kilowatt hour as the standard billing unit precisely because it accounts for both how powerful an appliance is and how long it runs, giving a fair measure of the actual energy used. Understanding this calculation allows a household to estimate their expected electricity bill in advance, and to identify which appliances are responsible for the largest share of their energy costs, supporting more informed decisions about energy conservation, as studied in Lessons 1 and 2.

pages.title: The Basic Parts of a Camera
pages.body: A lens, an aperture, a light sensitive surface, and a light tight body are the four basic parts found in essentially every camera, whether a simple pinhole camera, a traditional film camera, or a modern digital camera. The lens gathers and bends light rays coming from an object, the aperture is an adjustable opening that controls how much light enters, the light sensitive surface, either photographic film or a digital sensor, captures the resulting image, and the light tight body prevents any unwanted light from entering and spoiling the image.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How a Camera Forms an Image

pages.title: How a Camera Forms an Image
pages.body:
Light rays from an object outside the camera travel in straight lines until they reach the lens, which bends (refracts) these rays so that they converge and meet again at a point behind the lens, forming a focused image on the light sensitive surface. Because light rays from the top of an object cross over and end up at the bottom of the image, and rays from the bottom cross over to the top, the image formed inside a camera is upside down (inverted) compared with the actual object, though this is automatically corrected in modern digital cameras before the image is displayed or printed.

[[pic:A labelled ray diagram showing an object such as an arrow standing upright outside a simple camera, with straight light rays travelling from the top and bottom of the arrow through a labelled convex lens, crossing over, and forming an inverted (upside down) image of the arrow on a labelled light sensitive surface (film or sensor) inside the camera body.]]

Notice how the crossing over of light rays as they pass through the lens is what causes the image to appear upside down inside the camera, a principle shared by both simple pinhole cameras and more advanced lens based cameras.

pages.title: The Role of the Aperture
pages.body: The aperture controls the amount of light allowed to reach the light sensitive surface, working somewhat like the pupil of a human eye, studied in an earlier grade. A wider aperture allows more light in, useful in dim conditions, while a narrower aperture allows less light in, useful in very bright conditions, helping to avoid an image that is too overexposed or washed out.

pages.title: Focusing the Image
pages.body: Focusing involves adjusting the distance between the lens and the light sensitive surface, or adjusting the shape or position of the lens itself, so that light rays from the object converge precisely on the light sensitive surface, producing a sharp, clear image rather than a blurred one. If the light sensitive surface is positioned too close to or too far from the lens relative to where the light rays actually converge, the resulting image will appear out of focus.

pages.title: Building a Simple Camera Model
pages.body: A simple working model demonstrating how a camera forms an image can be built using a small box, a piece of tracing paper or greaseproof paper to act as the light sensitive surface, and a small hole or simple lens at the opposite end to act as the aperture and lens. Light from an object outside the box passes through the small opening, crosses over, and forms a faint, upside down image on the tracing paper, which can be viewed by looking into the box from behind the paper in a dimly lit area, directly demonstrating the same basic principle used in real cameras.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

The human eye works on broadly similar principles to a camera, with its own lens focusing light onto the light sensitive retina at the back of the eye, forming an inverted image that the brain then interprets and corrects, allowing us to perceive the world the right way up. Comparing the camera studied in this lesson with the structure of the eye, studied in earlier grades, can help reinforce understanding of both.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Discuss the terms umbra and penumbra in relation to the formation of shadows, and explain how they are formed.

pages.title: Why Shadows Form
pages.body: A shadow forms when an opaque object, one that does not allow light to pass through it, blocks light travelling from a light source, since light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around the object to reach the space directly behind it. The shape of a shadow generally follows the outline of the object blocking the light, though its size and sharpness depend on the size of the light source and the distance between the source, the object, and the surface the shadow falls on.

questions.q: A shadow forms mainly because
o: An opaque object blocks light travelling in straight lines
Light bends around every object completely
Sound waves are blocked by an object
Water absorbs all nearby light
questions.e: Why Shadows Form A shadow forms when an opaque object, one that does not allow light to pass through it, blocks light travelling from a light source, since light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around the object to…

pages.title: The Umbra
pages.body: The umbra is the darkest, most completely shadowed part of a shadow, formed in the region directly behind an object where absolutely no direct light from the light source can reach. Within the umbra, the object completely blocks the entire light source from view, which is why this central region appears fully dark.

pages.title: The Penumbra
pages.body:
The penumbra is the lighter, partially shadowed region surrounding the umbra, formed where only part of the light source is blocked by the object, while the remaining part of the light source is still visible and still reaching that area. Since some, but not all, light still reaches the penumbra, it appears as a partial shadow, lighter than the umbra but darker than the fully lit surrounding area.

[[pic:A labelled ray diagram showing a large light source, such as the Sun, an opaque object blocking some of its light, and the resulting shadow region divided into two labelled zones, a small, completely dark umbra directly behind the object, and a larger, lighter penumbra surrounding it, with light rays drawn showing which rays are completely blocked and which are only partially blocked.]]

Notice that the umbra is generally narrower and completely dark, while the penumbra is generally wider and only partially dark, since it still receives some direct light from part of the light source.

pages.title: Factors Affecting Shadow Formation
pages.body: The size of the light source, the distance between the light source and the object, and the distance between the object and the surface receiving the shadow are three factors that influence how large, how sharp, and how clearly divided into umbra and penumbra a shadow appears. A very small, point like light source tends to produce a sharp shadow with barely any penumbra, since almost every ray is either completely blocked or completely unblocked. A larger light source, such as the Sun or a wide fluorescent tube, tends to produce a more noticeable penumbra, since different parts of the source are blocked to different extents depending on the exact position behind the object.

This everyday observation is a simple, familiar example of the same principles of straight line light travel and shadow formation studied in this lesson, and understanding umbra and penumbra also provides a foundation for understanding the formation of eclipses, studied in the next lesson.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Use a model to illustrate how an eclipse is formed.

pages.title: What is an Eclipse?
pages.body: An eclipse occurs when one celestial body moves into the shadow of another, or passes directly between another body and the Sun, temporarily blocking some or all of the light that would normally reach an observer. Eclipses are a direct, large scale demonstration of the same shadow formation principles, including the umbra and penumbra, studied in Lesson 5, applied to the Sun, the Earth and the Moon.

questions.q: An eclipse occurs when
o: One celestial body moves into the shadow of, or blocks light from, another
The Earth stops rotating entirely
The Sun stops producing light completely
Two stars collide directly
questions.e: An eclipse occurs when one celestial body moves into the shadow of another, or passes directly between another body and the Sun, temporarily blocking some or all of the light that would normally reach an observer.

pages.title: Solar Eclipses
pages.body: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and the Earth, casting its shadow onto the Earth's surface and blocking some or all of the Sun's light from reaching observers within that shadow. Observers located within the Moon's umbra experience a total solar eclipse, during which the Sun appears completely blocked for a short time, while observers located within the surrounding penumbra experience a partial solar eclipse, during which only part of the Sun appears blocked.

pages.title: Lunar Eclipses
pages.body:
A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, casting the Earth's shadow onto the Moon's surface and blocking some or all of the sunlight that would otherwise reflect off the Moon and reach observers on Earth. When the Moon passes completely into the Earth's umbra, observers experience a total lunar eclipse, during which the Moon can appear dimmed and often reddish, while a Moon passing only into the Earth's penumbra experiences a more subtle partial lunar eclipse.

[[pic:Two labelled diagrams side by side, the first showing the Sun, Moon and Earth aligned with the Moon between the Sun and Earth, casting a shadow onto the Earth's surface, labelled Solar Eclipse, and the second showing the Sun, Earth and Moon aligned with the Earth between the Sun and Moon, casting a shadow onto the Moon's surface, labelled Lunar Eclipse, with umbra and penumbra regions labelled on both.]]

Notice the key difference between the two types of eclipse, in a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth, while in a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, and in both cases it is the relative positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon that determine whether, and what type of, an eclipse occurs.

pages.title: Modelling an Eclipse
pages.body: A simple physical model demonstrating eclipse formation can be built using a bright torch or lamp to represent the Sun, a small ball to represent the Moon, and a larger ball to represent the Earth. Moving the smaller ball between the light source and the larger ball, and observing where its shadow falls, demonstrates a solar eclipse, while moving the larger ball between the light source and the smaller ball, and observing where its shadow falls on the smaller ball, demonstrates a lunar eclipse.

pages.title: Why Eclipses Do Not Happen Every Month
pages.body: Although the Moon orbits the Earth roughly once a month, eclipses do not occur every month, because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted relative to the Earth's orbit around the Sun. This means the Sun, Earth and Moon only line up closely enough to produce an eclipse on the occasions when a new or full Moon coincides with the Moon crossing the plane of Earth's orbit, which happens only a few times a year, explaining why solar and lunar eclipses are relatively infrequent, notable events rather than monthly occurrences.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Scientists can predict eclipses with great accuracy, many years in advance, since the movements of the Sun, Earth and Moon follow highly regular, well understood patterns. This predictability has made eclipses valuable historically for astronomical study, and continues to attract scientific and public interest today, though observers are always advised never to look directly at a solar eclipse without proper eye protection, since this can cause serious eye damage.

pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Carry out a practical activity to show that light bends as it travels from one medium to another, for example a rod appearing bent in water, and deep water appearing shallower than its real depth.

pages.title: What is Refraction?
pages.body: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another transparent medium of different density, such as from air into water or from air into glass. This bending happens because light travels at different speeds in different media, slowing down as it enters a denser medium and speeding up again as it leaves a denser medium for a less dense one, and this change in speed causes the light ray to change direction at the boundary between the two media, unless it hits that boundary at a perfect right angle.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: A Rod Appearing Bent in Water

pages.title: A Rod Appearing Bent in Water
pages.body: When a straight rod or stick is partly placed in water, it appears bent or broken at the point where it enters the water's surface. This happens because light reflecting off the part of the rod below the water surface must refract as it travels from water into air on its way to an observer's eye, bending away from its original straight path, so that the underwater portion of the rod appears to be positioned differently from where it actually is, creating the illusion of a bend.

pages.title: Water Appearing Shallower Than It Really Is
pages.body:
Similarly, a swimming pool or river often appears shallower than its true depth when viewed from above the surface, again because light travelling from an object at the bottom of the water must refract as it passes from water into air, bending in a way that makes the object, and therefore the apparent depth of the water, appear closer to the surface than it truly is. This is an important safety consideration, since someone may misjudge how deep a body of water actually is based on its refracted appearance.

[[pic:Two side by side ray diagrams, the first showing a straight rod partly submerged in a glass of water, with light rays bending at the water surface and a dashed line showing the apparent, bent position of the rod as seen by an observer's eye, and the second showing an object resting at the true bottom of a container of water, with light rays bending at the surface and a dashed line showing the shallower, apparent position of the object as perceived by an observer above the water.]]

Notice that in both diagrams, the actual position of the object underwater and its apparent position, as perceived due to refraction, are different, with the apparent position always appearing closer to the surface, or shifted, compared with the true position.

pages.title: Carrying Out a Simple Refraction Activity
pages.body: Placing a straight pencil or rod into a clear glass of water at an angle, then observing it from the side, provides a simple, direct demonstration of refraction, since the pencil will appear to bend sharply at the point where it enters the water. Similarly, placing a coin at the bottom of an empty, opaque cup, positioning your eye so the coin is just out of sight over the rim, then slowly adding water to the cup without moving your head, demonstrates how the coin gradually becomes visible as the water refracts light from the coin over the rim of the cup, showing how refraction changes the apparent position of an underwater object.

pages.title: The Terms and Rules of Refraction
pages.body:
| **TERM** | **MEANING** |
|---|---|
| **Incident ray** | The ray of light that arrives at the boundary between two media |
| **Refracted ray** | The ray that continues in the second medium after bending |
| **Normal** | An imaginary line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray meets it |
| **Angle of incidence** | The angle between the incident ray and the normal |
| **Angle of refraction** | The angle between the refracted ray and the normal |

- Light bends because it travels at different speeds in different media. It travels fastest in air, more slowly in water and more slowly still in glass.

- When light passes from a less dense medium such as air into a denser medium such as water or glass, it slows down and bends towards the normal.

- When light passes from a denser medium into a less dense medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

- A ray that meets the boundary at right angles, along the normal, passes straight through without bending.

Refraction explains several everyday observations. A straight rod looks bent at the surface of water. A pond or a bucket of water looks shallower than it really is, because light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so the bottom appears raised. The depth that is seen is called the apparent depth and it is always less than the real depth. A coin at the bottom of an empty cup that cannot be seen from the side comes into view when water is poured in. Lenses in spectacles, cameras and the eye also work by refraction.

pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Refraction is not limited to water. It also occurs whenever light passes between any two transparent media of different density, including the air and glass of a lens, which is precisely the principle that allows a camera lens, studied in Lesson 4, and the human eye to bend and focus light to form an image.
